key_insight: In older adults, women showed greater brain activation than men during worry induction in regions linked to visual processing and emotion regulation, suggesting sex-specific neural pathways for worry.
clinical_relevance: These findings may help explain why chronic, hard-to-control worry is more common in older women and could inform future sex-aware approaches to assessing or targeting worry-related symptoms.
method: 131 older adults completed an in-scanner fMRI worry induction and reappraisal task.
Researchers compared sex differences with voxel-wise t-tests across task contrasts.
Regions showing differences were tested for links to worry severity and regulation strategies such as reappraisal and suppression.
evidence_signal: This was a task-based fMRI study with voxel-wise group comparisons and regression analyses linking regional activity to self-reported worry and regulation strategy use.
watch_item: The results are associative and based on a specific older-adult sample, so they do not establish causation or directly support clinical decision-making.
paper_title: Sex Differences in Neural Activity during Worry Induction and Reappraisal in Late Life
